That to attempt it, would be inevitably to be torn into a quick eternity. On this head, there are some remarkable documents that may be consulted.

Nevertheless, some there were, who even in the face of these things were ready to give chase to Moby Dick; and a still greater number who, chancing only to hear of him distantly and vaguely, without the specific details of any certain calamity, and without superstitious accompaniments, were sufficiently hardy not to flee from the battle if offered.

Nor, credulous as such minds must have been, was this conceit altogether without some faint show of superstitious probability. For as the secrets of the currents in the seas have never yet been divulged, even to the most erudite research; so the hidden ways of the Sperm Whale when beneath the surface remain, in great part, unaccountable to his pursuers; and from time to time have originated the most curious and contradictory speculations regarding them, especially concerning the mystic modes whereby, after sounding to a great depth, he transports himself with such vast swiftness to the most widely distant points.

It is a thing well known to both American and English whale-ships, and as well a thing placed upon authoritative record years ago by Scoresby, that some whales have been captured far north in the Pacific, in whose bodies have been found the barbs of harpoons darted in the Greenland seas. Nor is it to be gainsaid, that in some of these instances it has been declared that the interval of time between the two assaults could not have exceeded very many days. Hence, by inference, it has been believed by some whalemen, that the Nor’ West Passage, so long a problem to man, was never a problem to the whale. So that here, in the real living experience of living men, the prodigies related in old times of the inland Strello mountain in Portugal (near whose top there was said to be a lake in which the wrecks of ships floated up to the surface); and that still more wonderful story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse (whose waters were believed to have come from the Holy Land by an underground passage); these fabulous narrations are almost fully equalled by the realities of the whalemen.

Forced into familiarity, then, with such prodigies as these; and knowing that after repeated, intrepid assaults, the White Whale had escaped alive; it cannot be much matter of surprise that some whalemen should go still further in their superstitions; declaring Moby Dick not only ubiquitous, but immortal (for immortality is but ubiquity in time); that though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed; or if indeed he should ever be made to spout thick blood, such a sight would be but a ghastly deception; for again in unensanguined billows hundreds of leagues away, his unsullied jet would once more be seen.

But even stripped of these supernatural surmisings, there was enough in the earthly make and incontestable character of the monster to strike the imagination with unwonted power. For, it was not so much his uncommon bulk that so much distinguished him from other sperm whales, but, as was elsewhere thrown out—a peculiar snow-white wrinkled forehead, and a high, pyramidical white hump. These were his prominent features; the tokens whereby, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity, at a long distance, to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, and spotted, and marbled with the same shrouded hue, that, in the end, he had gained his distinctive appellation of the White Whale; a name, indeed, literally justified by his vivid aspect, when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all spangled with golden gleamings.

Nor was it his unwonted magnitude, nor his remarkable hue, nor yet his deformed lower jaw, that so much invested the whale with natural terror, as that unexampled, intelligent malignity which, according to specific accounts, he had over and over again evinced in his assaults. More than all, his treacherous retreats struck more of dismay than perhaps aught else. For, when swimming before his exulting pursuers, with every apparent symptom of alarm, he had several times been known to turn round suddenly, and, bearing down upon them, either stave their boats to splinters, or drive them back in consternation to their ship.

Already several fatalities had attended his chase. But though similar disasters, however little bruited ashore, were by no means unusual in the fishery; yet, in most instances, such seemed the White Whale’s infernal aforethought of ferocity, that every dismembering or death that he caused, was not wholly regarded as having been inflicted by an unintelligent agent.

Judge, then, to what pitches of inflamed, distracted fury the minds of his more desperate hunters were impelled, when amid the chips of chewed boats, and the sinking limbs of torn comrades, they swam out of the white curds of the whale’s direful wrath into the serene, exasperating sunlight, that smiled on, as if at a birth or a bridal.

His three boats stove around him, and oars and men both whirling in the eddies; one captain, seizing the line-knife from his broken prow, had dashed at the whale, as an Arkansas duellist at his foe, blindly seeking with a six inch blade to reach the fathom-deep life of the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was, that suddenly sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, Moby Dick had reaped away Ahab’s leg, as a mower a blade of grass in the field. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay, could have smote him with more seeming malice. Small reason was there to doubt, then, that ever since that almost fatal encounter, Ahab had cherished a wild vindictiveness against the whale, all the more fell for that in his frantic morbidness he at last came to identify with him, not only all his bodily woes, but all his intellectual and spiritual exasperations. The White Whale swam before him as the monomaniac incarnation of all those malicious agencies which some deep men feel eating in them, till they are left living on with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible malignity which has been from the beginning; to whose dominion even the modern Christians ascribe one-half of the worlds; which the ancient Ophites of the east reverenced in their statue devil;—Ahab did not fall down and worship it like them; but deliriously transferring its idea to the abhorred white whale, he pitted himself, all mutilated, against it. All that most maddens and torments; all that stirs up the lees of things; all truth with malice in it; all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain; all the subtle demonisms of life and thought; all evil, to crazy Ahab, were visibly personified, and made practically assailable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale’s white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down; and then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart’s shell upon it.

It is not probable that this monomania in him took its instant rise at the precise time of his bodily dismemberment. Then, in darting at the monster, knife in hand, he had but given loose to a sudden, passionate, corporal animosity; and when he received the stroke that tore him, he probably but felt the agonizing bodily laceration, but nothing more. Yet, when by this collision forced to turn towards home, and for long months of days and weeks, Ahab and anguish lay stretched together in one hammock, rounding in mid winter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape; then it was, that his torn body and gashed soul bled into one another; and so interfusing, made him mad. That it was only then, on the homeward voyage, after the encounter, that the final monomania seized him, seems all but certain from the fact that, at intervals during the passage, he was a raving lunatic; and, though unlimbed of a leg, yet such vital strength yet lurked in his Egyptian chest, and was moreover intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lace him fast, even there, as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a strait-jacket, he swung to the mad rockings of the gales. And, when running into more sufferable latitudes, the ship, with mild stun’sails spread, floated across the tranquil tropics, and, to all appearances, the old man’s delirium seemed left behind him with the Cape Horn swells, and he came forth from his dark den into the blessed light and air; even then, when he bore that firm, collected front, however pale, and issued his calm orders once again; and his mates thanked God the direful madness was now gone; even then, Ahab, in his hidden self, raved on. Human madness is oftentimes a cunning and most feline thing. When you think it fled, it may have but become transfigured into some still subtler form. Ahab’s full lunacy subsided not, but deepeningly contracted; like the unabated Hudson, when that noble Northman flows narrowly, but unfathomably through the Highland gorge. But, as in his narrow-flowing monomania, not one jot of Ahab’s broad madness had been left behind; so in that broad madness, not one jot of his great natural intellect had perished. That before living agent, now became the living instrument. If such a furious trope may stand, his special lunacy stormed his general sanity, and carried it, and turned all its concentred cannon upon its own mad mark; so that far from having lost his strength, Ahab, to that one end, did now possess a thousand fold more potency than ever he had sanely brought to bear upon any one reasonable object.

This is much; yet Ahab’s larger, darker, deeper part remains unhinted. But vain to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked Hotel de Cluny where we here stand—however grand and wonderful, now quit it;—and take your way, ye nobler, sadder souls, to those vast Roman halls of Thermes; where far beneath the fantastic towers of man’s upper earth, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits in bearded state; an antique buried beneath antiquities, and throned on torsoes! So with a broken throne, the great gods mock that captive king; so like a Caryatid, he patient sits, upholding on his frozen brow the piled entablatures of ages. Wind ye down there, ye prouder, sadder souls! question that proud, sad king! A family likeness! aye, he did beget ye, ye young exiled royalties; and from your grim sire only will the old State-secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this, namely: all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad. Yet without power to kill, or change, or shun the fact; he likewise knew that to mankind he did long dissemble; in some sort, did still. But that thing of his dissembling was only subject to his perceptibility, not to his will determinate. Nevertheless, so well did he succeed in that dissembling, that when with ivory leg he stepped ashore at last, no Nantucketer thought him otherwise than but naturally grieved, and that to the quick, with the terrible casualty which had overtaken him.

The report of his undeniable delirium at sea was likewise popularly ascribed to a kindred cause. And so too, all the added moodiness which always afterwards, to the very day of sailing in the Pequod on the present voyage, sat brooding on his brow. Nor is it so very unlikely, that far from distrusting his fitness for another whaling voyage, on account of such dark symptoms, the calculating people of that prudent isle were inclined to harbor the conceit, that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge, for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed within and scorched without, with the infixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea; such an one, could he be found, would seem the very man to dart his iron and lift his lance against the most appalling of all brutes. Or, if for any reason thought to be corporeally incapacitated for that, yet such an one would seem superlatively competent to cheer and howl on his underlings to the attack. But be all this as it may, certain it is, that with the mad secret of his unabated rage bolted up and keyed in him, Ahab had purposely sailed upon the present voyage with the one only and all-engrossing object of hunting the White Whale. Had any one of his old acquaintances on shore but half dreamed of what was lurking in him then, how soon would their aghast and righteous souls have wrenched the ship from such a fiendish man! They were bent on profitable cruises, the profit to be counted down in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, immitigable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this grey-headed, ungodly old man, chasing with curses a Job’s whale round the world, at the head of a crew, too, chiefly made up of mongrel renegades, and castaways, and cannibals—morally enfeebled also, by the incompetence of mere unaided virtue or right-mindedness in Starbuck, the invulnerable jollity of indifference and recklessness in Stubb, and the pervading mediocrity in Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially picked and packed by some infernal fatality to help him to his monomaniac revenge. How it was that they so aboundingly responded to the old man’s ire—by what evil magic their souls were possessed, that at times his hate seemed almost theirs; the White Whale as much their insufferable foe as his; how all this came to be—what the White Whale was to them, or how to their unconscious understandings, also, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life,—all this to explain, would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The subterranean miner that works in us all, how can one tell whither leads his shaft by the ever shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who does not feel the irresistible arm drag? What skiff in tow of a seventy-four can stand still? For one, I gave myself up to the abandonment of the time and the place; but while yet all a-rush to encounter the whale, could see naught in that brute but the deadliest ill.

Judge, then, to what pitches of inflamed, distracted fury the minds of his more desperate hunters were impelled, when amid the chips of chewed boats, and the sinking limbs of torn comrades, they swam out of the white curds of the whale’s direful wrath into the serene, exasperating sunlight, that smiled on, as if at a birth or a bridal.

His three boats stove around him, and oars and men both whirling in the eddies; one captain, seizing the line-knife from his broken prow, had dashed at the whale, as an Arkansas duellist at his foe, blindly seeking with a six inch blade to reach the fathom-deep life of the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was, that suddenly sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, Moby Dick had reaped away Ahab’s leg, as a mower a blade of grass in the field. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay, could have smote him with more seeming malice. Small reason was there to doubt, then, that ever since that almost fatal encounter, Ahab had cherished a wild vindictiveness against the whale, all the more fell for that in his frantic morbidness he at last came to identify with him, not only all his bodily woes, but all his intellectual and spiritual exasperations. The White Whale swam before him as the monomaniac incarnation of all those malicious agencies which some deep men feel eating in them, till they are left living on with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible malignity which has been from the beginning; to whose dominion even the modern Christians ascribe one-half of the worlds; which the ancient Ophites of the east reverenced in their statue devil;—Ahab did not fall down and worship it like them; but deliriously transferring its idea to the abhorred white whale, he pitted himself, all mutilated, against it. All that most maddens and torments; all that stirs up the lees of things; all truth with malice in it; all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain; all the subtle demonisms of life and thought; all evil, to crazy Ahab, were visibly personified, and made practically assailable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale’s white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down; and then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart’s shell upon it.

It is not probable that this monomania in him took its instant rise at the precise time of his bodily dismemberment. Then, in darting at the monster, knife in hand, he had but given loose to a sudden, passionate, corporal animosity; and when he received the stroke that tore him, he probably but felt the agonizing bodily laceration, but nothing more. Yet, when by this collision forced to turn towards home, and for long months of days and weeks, Ahab and anguish lay stretched together in one hammock, rounding in mid winter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape; then it was, that his torn body and gashed soul bled into one another; and so interfusing, made him mad. That it was only then, on the homeward voyage, after the encounter, that the final monomania seized him, seems all but certain from the fact that, at intervals during the passage, he was a raving lunatic; and, though unlimbed of a leg, yet such vital strength yet lurked in his Egyptian chest, and was moreover intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lace him fast, even there, as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a strait-jacket, he swung to the mad rockings of the gales. And, when running into more sufferable latitudes, the ship, with mild stun’sails spread, floated across the tranquil tropics, and, to all appearances, the old man’s delirium seemed left behind him with the Cape Horn swells, and he came forth from his dark den into the blessed light and air; even then, when he bore that firm, collected front, however pale, and issued his calm orders once again; and his mates thanked God the direful madness was now gone; even then, Ahab, in his hidden self, raved on. Human madness is oftentimes a cunning and most feline thing. When you think it fled, it may have but become transfigured into some still subtler form. Ahab’s full lunacy subsided not, but deepeningly contracted; like the unabated Hudson, when that noble Northman flows narrowly, but unfathomably through the Highland gorge. But, as in his narrow-flowing monomania, not one jot of Ahab’s broad madness had been left behind; so in that broad madness, not one jot of his great natural intellect had perished. That before living agent, now became the living instrument. If such a furious trope may stand, his special lunacy stormed his general sanity, and carried it, and turned all its concentred cannon upon its own mad mark; so that far from having lost his strength, Ahab, to that one end, did now possess a thousand fold more potency than ever he had sanely brought to bear upon any one reasonable object.

This is much; yet Ahab’s larger, darker, deeper part remains unhinted. But vain to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked Hotel de Cluny where we here stand—however grand and wonderful, now quit it;—and take your way, ye nobler, sadder souls, to those vast Roman halls of Thermes; where far beneath the fantastic towers of man’s upper earth, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits in bearded state; an antique buried beneath antiquities, and throned on torsoes! So with a broken throne, the great gods mock that captive king; so like a Caryatid, he patient sits, upholding on his frozen brow the piled entablatures of ages. Wind ye down there, ye prouder, sadder souls! question that proud, sad king! A family likeness! aye, he did beget ye, ye young exiled royalties; and from your grim sire only will the old State-secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this, namely: all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad. Yet without power to kill, or change, or shun the fact; he likewise knew that to mankind he did long dissemble; in some sort, did still. But that thing of his dissembling was only subject to his perceptibility, not to his will determinate. Nevertheless, so well did he succeed in that dissembling, that when with ivory leg he stepped ashore at last, no Nantucketer thought him otherwise than but naturally grieved, and that to the quick, with the terrible casualty which had overtaken him.

The report of his undeniable delirium at sea was likewise popularly ascribed to a kindred cause. And so too, all the added moodiness which always afterwards, to the very day of sailing in the Pequod on the present voyage, sat brooding on his brow. Nor is it so very unlikely, that far from distrusting his fitness for another whaling voyage, on account of such dark symptoms, the calculating people of that prudent isle were inclined to harbor the conceit, that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge, for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed within and scorched without, with the infixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea; such an one, could he be found, would seem the very man to dart his iron and lift his lance against the most appalling of all brutes. Or, if for any reason thought to be corporeally incapacitated for that, yet such an one would seem superlatively competent to cheer and howl on his underlings to the attack. But be all this as it may, certain it is, that with the mad secret of his unabated rage bolted up and keyed in him, Ahab had purposely sailed upon the present voyage with the one only and all-engrossing object of hunting the White Whale. Had any one of his old acquaintances on shore but half dreamed of what was lurking in him then, how soon would their aghast and righteous souls have wrenched the ship from such a fiendish man! They were bent on profitable cruises, the profit to be counted down in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, immitigable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this grey-headed, ungodly old man, chasing with curses a Job’s whale round the world, at the head of a crew, too, chiefly made up of mongrel renegades, and castaways, and cannibals—morally enfeebled also, by the incompetence of mere unaided virtue or right-mindedness in Starbuck, the invulnerable jollity of indifference and recklessness in Stubb, and the pervading mediocrity in Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially picked and packed by some infernal fatality to help him to his monomaniac revenge. How it was that they so aboundingly responded to the old man’s ire—by what evil magic their souls were possessed, that at times his hate seemed almost theirs; the White Whale as much their insufferable foe as his; how all this came to be—what the White Whale was to them, or how to their unconscious understandings, also, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life,—all this to explain, would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The subterranean miner that works in us all, how can one tell whither leads his shaft by the ever shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who does not feel the irresistible arm drag? What skiff in tow of a seventy-four can stand still? For one, I gave myself up to the abandonment of the time and the place; but while yet all a-rush to encounter the whale, could see naught in that brute but the deadliest ill.

modern_en.title: Chapter 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts had gone up with the rest. My oath had been welded with theirs. And I shouted louder and hammered my oath harder because of the dread in my soul. A wild, mystical, sympathetic feeling was in me. Ahab's unquenchable feud seemed like my own. With eager ears I learned the history of that murderous monster against whom I and all the others had sworn our oaths of violence and revenge.

For some time past, though only at intervals, the solitary, secluded White Whale had haunted those uncivilized seas mostly visited by the Sperm Whale hunters. But not all of them knew of his existence. Only a few, comparatively, had knowingly seen him, and the number who had actually and knowingly fought him was very small indeed. For many reasons — the large number of whale ships; the disorderly way they were scattered over the entire watery globe, many of them adventurously pushing their hunt along lonely latitudes, so that for a whole year or more at a stretch they might seldom or never meet a single sail of any sort that could tell them news; the extreme length of each voyage; the irregular times of sailing from home — all these, with other circumstances direct and indirect, had long prevented the specific news about Moby Dick as an individual from spreading through the whole worldwide whaling fleet. Several ships were reported to have encountered, at such and such a time or on such and such a meridian, a Sperm Whale of unusual size and malignity which, after doing great damage to its attackers, had completely escaped them; it could hardly be doubted — to some minds, I say, it was not an unfair assumption — that this whale must have been none other than Moby Dick. Yet since the Sperm Whale fishery had lately seen various and not infrequent instances of great ferocity, cunning, and malice in the whale under attack, those who by accident unknowingly fought Moby Dick were perhaps, for the most part, content to blame the peculiar terror he inspired more, as it were, on the dangers of the Sperm Whale fishery at large than on the individual cause. That, mostly, was how the disastrous encounter between Ahab and the whale had so far been popularly regarded.

As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or devouring amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who later heard the story of the White Whale.

Nor did wild rumors of all kinds fail to exaggerate the true accounts of these deadly encounters and make them still more horrifying. For not only do fantastic rumors naturally grow out of the very body of all surprising, terrible events, as a stricken tree gives birth to its fungi, but in life at sea, far more than on dry land, wild rumors abound wherever there is any adequate reality for them to cling to. And just as the sea surpasses the land in this respect, so the whale fishery surpasses every other kind of seafaring life in the wonder and fearfulness of the rumors that sometimes circulate there. For whalemen as a body are not exempt from the ignorance and superstition that all sailors inherit; but of all sailors, they are by far the most directly brought into contact with whatever is appallingly astonishing in the sea. Face to face they not only see its greatest marvels, but, hand to jaw, they fight them. Alone, in waters so remote that you could sail a thousand miles and pass a thousand shores without coming to a single chiseled hearthstone, or anything hospitable beneath that part of the sun — in such latitudes and longitudes, and pursuing such a calling as he does, the whaleman is wrapped in influences that all tend to make his imagination pregnant with many a mighty birth.

No wonder, then, that as the rumors of the White Whale kept gathering bulk from merely crossing the widest ocean spaces, they finally absorbed all manner of morbid hints and half-formed, fetal suggestions of supernatural forces, which in the end invested Moby Dick with new terrors borrowed from nothing that visibly appears. So in many cases he finally struck such a panic that, of those who had heard of the White Whale — through those rumors, at least — few of those hunters were willing to face the dangers of his jaw.

But there were still other, more vital practical influences at work. Even today, the original prestige of the Sperm Whale, as fearfully distinguished from all other species of leviathan, has not died out of the minds of whalemen as a body. There are those among them today who, though intelligent and brave enough to give battle to the Greenland or right whale, would perhaps — from lack of professional experience, or incompetence, or timidity — decline a contest with the Sperm Whale. At any rate, there are plenty of whalemen, especially among the whaling nations not sailing under the American flag, who have never met the Sperm Whale in battle, and whose only knowledge of the leviathan is limited to the ignoble monster originally hunted in the North. Seated on their hatches, these men will listen with a childlike fireside interest and awe to the wild, strange tales of southern whaling. And nowhere is the supreme tremendousness of the great Sperm Whale more deeply felt and understood than aboard the ships whose bows breast him.

And as if the now proven reality of his power had, in earlier legendary times, cast its shadow before it, we find some book naturalists — Olassen and Povelson — declaring the Sperm Whale not only to be a terror to every other creature in the sea but so incredibly ferocious as to be continually thirsting for human blood. Even as late as Cuvier's time, these or very similar impressions had not been erased. For in his Natural History, the Baron himself states that at the sight of the Sperm Whale, all fish (sharks included) are "struck with the most lively terrors," and "often in the precipitancy of their flight dash themselves against the rocks with such violence as to cause instantaneous death." And however much the general experience of the fishery may correct such reports, in their full terribleness — even down to Povelson's bloodthirsty detail — the superstitious belief in them is, in some turns of fortune in their calling, revived in the hunters' minds.

So, overawed by the rumors and portents concerning him, not a few of the fishermen recalled, in connection with Moby Dick, the earlier days of the Sperm Whale fishery, when it was often hard to persuade long-practiced right whalemen to embark on the perils of this new and daring warfare. Such men protested that although other leviathans might be pursued with hope of success, to chase and point a lance at such an apparition as the Sperm Whale was not for mortal man. To attempt it would inevitably mean being torn into a quick eternity. On this point, there are some remarkable documents that may be consulted.

Nevertheless, some there were who, even knowing all this, were ready to chase Moby Dick. And an even greater number, having only heard of him vaguely and at a distance, without specific details of any particular disaster and without the superstitious trappings, were tough enough not to flee from the fight if it came to them.

One of the wild ideas I mentioned, which eventually became linked with the White Whale in superstitious minds, was the eerie notion that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had actually been encountered in opposite latitudes at the very same instant.

Nor, credulous as such minds must have been, was this idea altogether without some faint show of superstitious probability. For since the secrets of the ocean currents have never yet been revealed, even to the most learned research, the hidden ways of the Sperm Whale beneath the surface remain, in great part, unaccountable to his pursuers. From time to time they have given rise to the most curious and contradictory speculations, especially about the mystic means by which, after sounding to a great depth, he transports himself with such vast swiftness to the most widely distant points.

It is well known to both American and English whale ships, and was also placed on authoritative record years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with the barbs of harpoons thrown in the Greenland seas still in their bodies. Nor can it be denied that in some of these cases it has been declared that the time between the two attacks could not have been very many days. Hence, by inference, some whalemen have believed that the Northwest Passage, so long a problem to man, was never a problem to the whale. So that here, in the real living experience of living men, the wonders told in old times of the inland Strello mountain in Portugal (near whose top there was said to be a lake in which the wrecks of ships floated up to the surface), and that still more wonderful story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse (whose waters were believed to have come from the Holy Land by an underground passage) — these fabulous tales are almost fully equaled by the realities of the whalemen.

Forced into familiarity with such wonders, then, and knowing that after repeated, fearless attacks the White Whale had escaped alive, it can hardly be surprising that some whalemen went still further in their superstitions. They declared Moby Dick not only everywhere at once but immortal (for immortality is only being everywhere in time). Though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed. Or if indeed he should ever be made to spout thick blood, that sight would be only a ghastly deception. For again, in unbloodied waves hundreds of leagues away, his unstained spout would be seen once more.

But even stripped of these supernatural rumors, there was enough in the earthly reality and undeniable character of the monster to strike the imagination with extraordinary power. It was not so much his uncommon size that distinguished him from other sperm whales, but — as mentioned elsewhere — a peculiar snow-white, wrinkled forehead and a high, pyramid-shaped white hump. These were his prominent features, the marks by which, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity at a great distance to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, spotted, and marbled with the same ghostly hue that he had earned his distinctive name of the White Whale. A name literally justified by his vivid appearance when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all sparkling with golden gleams.

It was not his unusual size, nor his remarkable color, nor even his deformed lower jaw that invested the whale with such natural terror, but rather an unprecedented, intelligent malice that, according to specific accounts, he had displayed over and over in his attacks. Most of all, his treacherous retreats struck more fear than perhaps anything else. For when swimming ahead of his triumphant pursuers, showing every sign of alarm, he had been known several times to turn around suddenly and, bearing down on them, either smash their boats to splinters or drive them back in panic to their ship.

Several deaths had already attended his chase. Though similar disasters, however little talked about on shore, were by no means unusual in the fishery, in most cases the White Whale's ferocity seemed so infernal and premeditated that every maiming or death he caused was not wholly regarded as the work of an unintelligent agent.

Judge, then, what heights of inflamed, frantic fury the minds of his more desperate hunters were driven to when, among the splinters of chewed-up boats and the sinking limbs of torn-apart comrades, they swam out of the white curds of the whale's terrible wrath into the calm, infuriating sunlight, which went on smiling as if at a birth or a wedding.

His three boats stove in around him, and oars and men both whirling in the eddies, one captain had seized the line-knife from his broken bow and dashed at the whale like an Arkansas duelist at his enemy, blindly trying with a six-inch blade to reach the fathom-deep life of the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was that Moby Dick, suddenly sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, reaped away Ahab's leg as a mower cuts a blade of grass in the field. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay, could have struck him with more apparent malice. There was little reason to doubt, then, that ever since that nearly fatal encounter, Ahab had nursed a wild vindictiveness against the whale — all the more deadly because in his frantic morbidness he at last came to identify with him not only all his bodily woes but all his intellectual and spiritual torments. The White Whale swam before him as the monomaniac incarnation of all those malicious forces that some deep men feel eating away inside them, until they are left living on with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible malignity which has existed from the beginning — to whose rule even modern Christians assign one half of the worlds, and which the ancient Ophites of the East revered in their statue devil — Ahab did not fall down and worship it as they did. Instead, deliriously transferring its idea to the hated white whale, he pitted himself, all mutilated, against it. All that most maddens and torments, all that stirs up the dregs of things, all truth with malice in it, all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain, all the subtle demonisms of life and thought — all evil, to crazy Ahab, was visibly personified and made practically assailable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale's white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down. And then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart's shell upon it.

It is not probable that this monomania in him arose at the precise moment of his bodily dismemberment. Then, in darting at the monster, knife in hand, he had only given way to a sudden, passionate, physical animosity. And when he received the stroke that tore him, he probably felt only the agonizing bodily laceration, and nothing more. Yet when, forced by this collision to turn toward home, Ahab and anguish lay stretched together in one hammock for long months of days and weeks, rounding in midwinter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape — then it was that his torn body and gashed soul bled into one another, and, so mingling, made him mad. That it was only then, on the homeward voyage after the encounter, that the final monomania seized him seems all but certain from the fact that at intervals during the passage he was a raving lunatic. And though he had lost a leg, such vital strength still lurked in his Egyptian chest, further intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lash him fast, even there, as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a straitjacket he swung to the mad rocking of the gales. And when, running into more bearable latitudes, the ship floated across the tranquil tropics with mild studding sails spread, and to all appearances the old man's delirium seemed left behind him with the Cape Horn swells, and he came out of his dark den into the blessed light and air — even then, when he showed that firm, collected face, however pale, and gave his calm orders once again, and his mates thanked God the dreadful madness was now gone — even then, Ahab, in his hidden self, raved on. Human madness is often a cunning and most catlike thing. When you think it has fled, it may only have been transfigured into some still subtler form. Ahab's full lunacy did not subside but contracted and deepened, like the undiminished Hudson when that noble Northman flows narrowly but unfathomably through the Highland gorge. And just as in his narrow-flowing monomania not one jot of Ahab's broad madness had been left behind, so in that broad madness not one jot of his great natural intellect had perished. What had been the living agent now became the living instrument. If such a violent figure of speech may stand, his special lunacy stormed his general sanity and carried it, and turned all its concentrated cannon on its own mad target. So far from having lost his strength, Ahab, for that one end, now possessed a thousand times more power than he had ever sanely brought to bear on any one reasonable object.

This is much; yet Ahab's larger, darker, deeper part remains not even hinted at. But it is vain to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked Hotel de Cluny where we now stand — however grand and wonderful, leave it now — take your way, you nobler, sadder souls, to those vast Roman halls of the Thermes (the ancient baths beneath it), where far below the fantastic towers of man's upper earth, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits in bearded state: an antique buried beneath antiquities, and throned on torsos! So, with a broken throne, the great gods mock that captive king; so, like a Caryatid (a carved figure serving as a column), he sits patiently, holding up on his frozen brow the piled entablatures of ages. Wind your way down there, you prouder, sadder souls! Question that proud, sad king! A family likeness! Yes, he begat you, you young exiled royalties; and from your grim father alone will the old state secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this — namely: all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad. Yet without power to kill, change, or escape the fact, he also knew that he had long been deceiving mankind about it — and in some ways still was. But his deception was only subject to his awareness, not to his deliberate will. Nevertheless, he succeeded so well in it that when he stepped ashore on his ivory leg at last, no Nantucketer thought him anything other than naturally grief-stricken, and deeply so, by the terrible accident that had befallen him.

The reports of his undeniable delirium at sea were likewise popularly put down to a related cause. And so too was all the added moodiness that always afterward, right up to the day of sailing in the Pequod on the present voyage, sat brooding on his brow. And it is not so very unlikely that, far from doubting his fitness for another whaling voyage because of such dark symptoms, the calculating people of that prudent island were inclined to entertain the notion that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed within and scorched without by the fixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea — such a man, if he could be found, would seem the very man to dart his iron and lift his lance against the most appalling of all brutes. Or, if for any reason he were thought physically unfit for that, such a man would seem supremely qualified to cheer and howl his underlings on to the attack. But be all this as it may, this much is certain: with the mad secret of his unabated rage bolted up and locked inside him, Ahab had deliberately sailed on the present voyage with the one sole, all-consuming object of hunting the White Whale. Had any one of his old acquaintances on shore even half dreamed of what was lurking in him then, how quickly their aghast and righteous souls would have wrenched the ship from such a fiendish man! They were bent on profitable cruises, the profit to be counted down in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, implacable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this gray-headed, ungodly old man, chasing with curses a Job's whale around the world, at the head of a crew, too, made up chiefly of mongrel renegades, and castaways, and cannibals — a crew morally weakened as well by the helplessness of mere unaided virtue or right-mindedness in Starbuck, the invulnerable jollity of indifference and recklessness in Stubb, and the pervading mediocrity in Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially picked and packed by some infernal fate to help him to his monomaniac revenge. How it was that they responded so abundantly to the old man's fury — by what evil magic their souls were possessed, so that at times his hate seemed almost theirs, and the White Whale as much their unbearable enemy as his — how all this came to be — what the White Whale was to them, or how, to their unconscious understandings as well, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life — to explain all this would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. modern_da.title: Kapitel 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: Jeg, Ishmael, var en af den besætning. Mine råb var gået op sammen med de andres. Min ed var blevet svejset sammen med deres. Og jeg råbte højere og hamrede min ed hårdere fast på grund af rædslen i min sjæl. En vild, mystisk, medfølende følelse rørte sig i mig. Ahabs uslukkelige fejde forekom mig som min egen. Med ivrige ører lærte jeg historien om det morderiske uhyre, som jeg og alle de andre havde svoret vold og hævn.

I nogen tid, dog kun med mellemrum, havde den ensomme, tilbagetrukne Hvide Hval hjemsøgt de vilde have, som mest besøges af kaskelotfangerne. Men ikke alle af dem kendte til hans eksistens. Kun nogle få havde forholdsvis bevidst set ham, og tallet på dem, der faktisk og bevidst havde kæmpet mod ham, var meget lille. Der var mange grunde til, at de specifikke nyheder om Moby Dick som enkeltindivid i så lang tid ikke havde spredt sig gennem hele den verdensomspændende hvalfangerflåde. Der var det store antal hvalfangerskibe. Der var den uordentlige måde, de var spredt ud over hele den vandfyldte klode på, og mange af dem gik eventyrligt på jagt langs ensomme breddegrader, så de i et helt år eller mere ad gangen sjældent eller aldrig mødte så meget som ét sejl af nogen art, der kunne give dem nyt. Der var hver enkelt rejses ekstreme længde. Der var de uregelmæssige tidspunkter, de sejlede hjemmefra på. Alt dette, sammen med andre omstændigheder, direkte og indirekte, havde længe forhindret, at de bestemte nyheder om Moby Dick som individ bredte sig gennem hele den verdensomspændende hvalfangerflåde. Flere skibe blev rapporteret at have mødt, på det og det tidspunkt eller på den og den meridian, en kaskelot af usædvanlig størrelse og ondskab, som efter at have gjort stor skade på sine angribere var sluppet helt fra dem. Man kunne næppe tvivle på — for nogle sind, siger jeg, var det ikke en urimelig antagelse — at denne hval måtte have været ingen anden end Moby Dick. Men da kaskelotfangsten på det seneste havde set forskellige og ikke sjældne tilfælde af stor vildskab, list og ondskab hos den hval, der blev angrebet, var de, der ved et tilfælde og uden at vide det kæmpede mod Moby Dick, måske for det meste tilfredse med at skyde skylden for den særlige rædsel, han vakte, snarere, så at sige, på kaskelotfangstens farer i almindelighed end på den enkelte årsag. Sådan var det for det meste, at det skæbnesvangre sammenstød mellem Ahab og hvalen indtil nu var blevet set i folks øjne.

Hvad angår dem, der tidligere havde hørt om den Hvide Hval og så tilfældigvis fik øje på ham — i begyndelsen havde næsten alle af dem sat bådene ud efter ham lige så dristigt og uforfærdet som efter enhver anden kaskelot. Men med tiden fulgte der sådanne katastrofer af disse angreb — ikke bare forstuvede håndled og ankler, brækkede lemmer eller opslugende amputationer, men dødsfald af den dødeligste slags — at disse gentagne, ødelæggende nederlag, der alle lagde deres rædsler oven på Moby Dick, langt hen ad vejen havde rystet modet hos mange tapre fangstmænd, som siden hørte historien om den Hvide Hval.

Og vilde rygter af alle slags undlod heller ikke at overdrive de sande beretninger om disse dødelige sammenstød og gøre dem endnu mere skrækindjagende. For fantastiske rygter vokser ikke blot naturligt ud af selve kroppen på alle overraskende, frygtelige begivenheder, som et ramt træ føder sine svampe, men på havet florerer vilde rygter langt mere end på land, så snart der er en tilstrækkelig virkelighed, de kan klamre sig til. Og ligesom havet i den henseende overgår landet, overgår hvalfangsten alle andre former for sømandsliv i de forunderlige og frygtindgydende rygter, der nogle gange går på den. For hvalfangere som gruppe er ikke fri for den uvidenhed og overtro, som alle sømænd arver; men af alle sømænd er de langt de mest direkte i berøring med alt det, der er skræmmende vidunderligt i havet. Ansigt til ansigt ser de ikke bare havets største undere, men hånd mod kæbe kæmper de mod dem. Alene, i farvande så fjerne, at man kunne sejle tusind engelske mil og forbi tusind kyster uden at møde så meget som én tilhugget arnesten eller noget som helst gæstfrit under denne del af solen — i sådanne bredde- og længdegrader og med sådan et erhverv som hans er hvalfangeren omsluttet af påvirkninger, der alle får hans fantasi til at gå svanger med mangen en vældig fødsel.

Det er derfor ingen under, at rygterne om den Hvide Hval, efterhånden som de voksede i omfang bare ved at krydse de bredeste havstrækninger, til sidst optog alle slags sygelige antydninger og halvfærdige, spirende forestillinger om overnaturlige kræfter, som til sidst iklædte Moby Dick nye rædsler, lånt fra intet, der kan ses. Således vakte han i mange tilfælde til sidst sådan en panik, at af dem, der havde hørt om den Hvide Hval — i hvert fald gennem de rygter — var der kun få af hvalfangerne, som ville trodse farerne ved hans kæbe.

Men der var stadig andre, mere afgørende og praktiske påvirkninger på spil. Selv i dag er kaskelottens oprindelige prestige, hvormed den på skræmmende vis adskilte sig fra alle andre arter af havuhyrer, ikke uddød i hvalfangernes sind som gruppe. Der findes blandt dem i dag nogle, som, selv om de er kloge og modige nok til at give kamp til grønlandshvalen eller rethvalen, måske — af mangel på faglig erfaring, af uduelighed eller af frygtsomhed — ville afslå en kamp med kaskelotten. Under alle omstændigheder er der masser af hvalfangere, især blandt de hvalfangernationer, der ikke sejler under amerikansk flag, som aldrig har mødt kaskelotten i kamp, og hvis eneste kendskab til havuhyret er begrænset til det uædle monster, som oprindelig blev jaget i nord. Siddende på lugerne lytter disse mænd med barnlig interesse og ærefrygt, som ved kaminen, til de vilde, mærkelige fortællinger om hvalfangsten i syd. Og ingen steder mærkes og forstås den store kaskelots yderste vældighed dybere end om bord på de skibe, hvis stævne skærer sig ind mod ham.

Og som om hans nu beviste magt allerede i ældre, sagnomspundne tider havde kastet sin skygge forud, finder vi nogle boglige naturforskere — Olassen og Povelson — der erklærer, at kaskelotten ikke blot er en rædsel for alle andre skabninger i havet, men så utroligt grusom, at den hele tiden tørster efter menneskeblod. Selv så sent som på Cuviers tid var disse eller meget lignende forestillinger ikke blevet udryddet. For i sin Naturhistorie siger baronen selv, at ved synet af kaskelotten bliver alle fisk (hajer iberegnet) »slået med de mest levende rædsler«, og »kaster sig ofte i hastværket under deres flugt mod klipperne med en sådan voldsomhed, at det forårsager øjeblikkelig død«. Og hvor meget fangstens almindelige erfaring end korrigerer sådanne beretninger i deres fulde gru — selv ned til Povelsons blodtørstige detalje — bliver troen på dem, når lykken i deres erhverv vender sig, af og til vakt til live igen i fangernes sind.

Overvældede af rygterne og varslerne om ham kom ikke så få af fiskerne derfor til at tænke på, i forbindelse med Moby Dick, de tidligere dage i kaskelotfangsten, hvor det ofte var svært at overtale rethvalfangere med mange års erfaring til at begive sig ud i farerne ved denne nye og dristige krigsførelse. Sådanne mænd hævdede, at selv om andre havuhyrer måske kunne jages med håb om held, var det ikke noget for dødelige mennesker at forfølge og sigte med en lanse mod sådan et spøgelse som kaskelotten. At forsøge det ville uvægerligt betyde at blive revet ind i en hurtig evighed. På dette punkt findes der nogle bemærkelsesværdige dokumenter, som man kan slå op i.

Alligevel var der nogle, som, selv om de vidste alt dette, var parate til at jage Moby Dick. Og et endnu større antal, som kun havde hørt om ham løst og på afstand, uden nærmere enkeltheder om nogen bestemt ulykke og uden overtroens udsmykning, var hårde nok til ikke at flygte fra kampen, hvis den kom til dem.

En af de vilde forestillinger, jeg nævnte, og som til sidst blev knyttet til den hvide hval i overtroiske sind, var den uhyggelige tanke, at Moby Dick var overalt på én gang — at han faktisk var blevet truffet i modsatte breddegrader i netop samme øjeblik.

Og, så godtroende som sådanne sind må have været, var denne tanke heller ikke helt uden et svagt skær af overtroisk sandsynlighed. For da havstrømmenes hemmeligheder aldrig endnu er blevet afsløret, selv ikke for den lærdeste forskning, forbliver kaskelottens skjulte veje under overfladen for en stor dels vedkommende uforklarlige for dem, der jager den. Fra tid til anden har de givet anledning til de mest besynderlige og modstridende gisninger, især om de mystiske midler, hvormed han, efter at være dykket til en stor dybde, med så vældig hast flytter sig til de mest vidt adskilte steder.

Det er velkendt både på amerikanske og engelske hvalfangerskibe, og det blev for mange år siden også nedfældet som autoritativ oplysning af Scoresby, at nogle hvaler, der er fanget langt mod nord i Stillehavet, er blevet fundet med modhagerne fra harpuner, kastet i Grønlandshavet, endnu siddende i kroppen. Det kan heller ikke nægtes, at det i nogle af disse tilfælde er blevet erklæret, at tiden mellem de to angreb ikke kan have været mange dage. Derfor har nogle hvalfangere ud fra dette sluttet, at Nordvestpassagen, så længe et problem for mennesket, aldrig var et problem for hvalen. Så her, i levende menneskers virkelige, levende erfaring, bliver de undere, som man i gamle dage fortalte om Strello-bjerget inde i landet i Portugal (nær hvis top der skulle være en sø, hvor skibsvrag flød op til overfladen), og den endnu mere vidunderlige historie om Arethusa-kilden nær Syrakus (hvis vand man mente kom fra Det Hellige Land gennem en underjordisk gang) — disse eventyrlige fortællinger bliver næsten fuldt ud opvejet af hvalfangernes virkelighed.

Tvunget ind i fortrolighed med sådanne undere, og vel vidende at den hvide hval efter gentagne, uforfærdede angreb var sluppet levende væk, er det næppe overraskende, at nogle hvalfangere gik endnu videre i deres overtro. De erklærede Moby Dick ikke blot for at være overalt på én gang, men for udødelig (for udødelighed er blot at være overalt i tiden). Selv om der blev plantet lunde af spyd i hans sider, ville han stadig svømme uskadt væk. Eller hvis han nogensinde virkelig blev bragt til at sprøjte tykt blod, ville det syn kun være et uhyggeligt bedrag. For igen, i blodløse bølger hundreder af mil væk, ville hans pletfri sprøjt blive set endnu en gang.

Men selv renset for disse overnaturlige rygter var der nok i monstrets jordiske virkelighed og ubestridelige væsen til at ramme fantasien med ekstraordinær kraft. Det var ikke så meget hans usædvanlige størrelse, der adskilte ham fra andre kaskelotter, som — som nævnt andetsteds — en ejendommelig sneblændende, rynket pande og en høj, pyramideformet hvid pukkel. Det var hans fremtrædende kendetegn, de mærker, hvormed han, selv i de grænseløse, ukortlagte have, røbede sin identitet på lang afstand for dem, der kendte ham.

Resten af hans krop var så stribet, plettet og marmoreret med den samme spøgelsesagtige farve, at han havde fortjent sit særlige navn, den hvide hval. Et navn, der bogstaveligt blev retfærdiggjort af hans levende udseende, når man så ham glide ved højlys middag gennem et mørkeblåt hav og efterlade et mælkevejsspor af cremet skum, alt sammen glitrende af gyldne glimt.

Det var ikke hans usædvanlige størrelse, ej heller hans bemærkelsesværdige farve, ja ikke engang hans vanskabte underkæbe, der iklædte hvalen sådan en naturlig skræk, men snarere en hidtil uset, intelligent ondskab, som han ifølge nøjagtige beretninger igen og igen havde vist i sine angreb. Mest af alt skræmte hans forræderiske tilbagetog måske mere end noget andet. For når han svømmede foran sine triumferende forfølgere og viste alle tegn på rædsel, var han flere gange kendt for pludselig at vende om og, med kurs lige mod dem, enten knuse deres både til splinter eller drive dem forskrækkede tilbage til deres skib.

Flere dødsfald havde allerede fulgt jagten på ham. Selv om lignende ulykker, hvor lidt der end blev talt om dem på land, på ingen måde var usædvanlige i fangsten, syntes den hvide hvals voldsomhed i de fleste tilfælde så infernalsk og overlagt, at enhver lemlæstelse eller død, han forårsagede, ikke helt blev anset for en uintelligent kraft.

Døm så selv, til hvilke højder af ophidset, rasende vrede sindet hos hans mest desperate jægere blev drevet, når de blandt splinterne af opædte både og de synkende lemmer af sønderrevne kammerater svømmede ud af den hvide ostemasse af hvalens frygtelige vrede og ind i det rolige, provokerende sollys, som blev ved med at smile, som til en fødsel eller et bryllup.

Med sine tre både knust omkring sig, og årer og mænd begge hvirvlende rundt i strømhvirvlerne, havde en kaptajn grebet linekniven fra sin knuste stævn og kastet sig mod hvalen som en duellant fra Arkansas mod sin fjende, og forsøgte blindt med en seks tommer lang klinge at nå hvalens livsnerve, en favn nede. Den kaptajn var Ahab. Og det var da, at Moby Dick, der pludselig fejede sin seglformede underkæbe ind under sig, høstede Ahabs ben væk, som en slåmand skærer et græsstrå på marken. Ingen turbanklædt tyrk, ingen lejet venetianer eller malaj kunne have ramt ham med mere åbenlys ondskab. Der var derfor ringe grund til at tvivle på, at Ahab lige siden det næsten dødelige møde havde næret en vild hævngerrighed mod hvalen — så meget desto farligere, fordi han i sin hektiske sygelighed til sidst kom til at identificere ham med ikke blot alle sine legemlige lidelser, men også alle sine åndelige og sjælelige kvaler. Den hvide hval svømmede foran ham som den monomane legemliggørelse af alle de ondsindede kræfter, som nogle dybe mennesker føler æde sig op indeni, til de bliver efterladt til at leve videre med et halvt hjerte og en halv lunge. Den uhåndgribelige ondskab, som har eksisteret fra begyndelsen — til hvis herredømme selv moderne kristne tillægger den ene halvdel af verdener, og som de gamle ofitter i Østen dyrkede i deres djævlestatue — faldt Ahab ikke på knæ for og tilbad, som de gjorde. I stedet overførte han i sit vanvid dens idé til den forhadte hvide hval og stillede sig, helt lemlæstet, op imod den. Alt det, der mest gør rasende og piner, alt det, der rører op i tingenes bundfald, al sandhed med ondskab i sig, alt det, der knækker sener og stivner hjernen, alle livets og tankens snigende dæmonier — alt ondt var for den gale Ahab synligt legemliggjort og gjort praktisk angribeligt i Moby Dick. Han stablede på hvalens hvide pukkel summen af al det almindelige raseri og had, som hele hans slægt fra Adam og nedefter havde følt. Og så sprængte han, som om hans bryst havde været en mortér, sit varme hjertes granat mod den.

Det er ikke sandsynligt, at denne monomani opstod hos ham i selve det øjeblik, han blev lemlæstet. Dengang havde han, da han fór mod monstret med kniven i hånden, kun givet efter for en pludselig, lidenskabelig, fysisk fjendskab. Og da han modtog det slag, der rev ham itu, mærkede han sandsynligvis kun den pinefulde legemlige flænsning, og ikke andet. Men da Ahab og smerten, tvunget af dette sammenstød til at vende hjemad, lå strakt ud sammen i én hængekøje i lange måneder, uger og dage, mens de rundede det dystre, hylende Kap Horn midt om vinteren — da var det, at hans sønderrevne krop og flængede sjæl blødte ind i hinanden og i denne blanding gjorde ham gal. At det kun var da, på hjemrejsen efter mødet, at den endelige monomani greb ham, synes næsten sikkert ud fra det faktum, at han med mellemrum under overfarten var en rasende sindssyg. Og selv om han havde mistet et ben, lurede der stadig sådan en livskraft i hans egyptiske bryst, yderligere forøget af hans delirium, at hans styrmænd var tvunget til at binde ham fast, selv dér, mens han sejlede, rasende i sin hængekøje. I spændetrøje svingede han til stormenes vanvittige vuggen. Og da skibet, efter at være sejlet ind i mere udholdelige breddegrader, gled hen over de rolige tropiske have med milde studsejl sat, og alt tydede på, at den gamle mands delirium var blevet efterladt bag ham med dønningerne ved Kap Horn, og han kom ud af sin mørke hule og ind i det velsignede lys og den friske luft — selv da, da han viste det faste, samlede ansigt, hvor bleg det end var, og igen gav sine rolige ordrer, og hans styrmænd takkede Gud for, at det frygtelige vanvid nu var forbi — selv da blev Ahab i sit skjulte indre ved med at rave. Menneskets vanvid er ofte en snu og højst kattelignende ting. Når man tror, det er flygtet, kan det blot være blevet forvandlet til en endnu subtilere form. Ahabs fulde galskab aftog ikke, men trak sig sammen og blev dybere, som den uformindskede Hudson, når den ædle nordboer flyder smalt, men bundløst gennem højlandets kløft. Og ligesom der i hans smalt strømmende monomani ikke var efterladt det mindste af Ahabs brede galskab, så var der i den brede galskab ikke gået det mindste til grunde af hans store, naturlige intellekt. Det, der havde været den levende drivkraft, blev nu det levende redskab. Hvis så voldsom en talemåde må stå, stormede hans særlige galskab hans almindelige fornuft og bar den af sted og vendte hele dens samlede kanonild mod sit eget vanvittige mål. Langt fra at have mistet sin styrke besad Ahab nu, til det ene formål, tusind gange mere kraft, end han nogensinde ved sans og samling havde sat ind på noget fornuftigt mål.

Det er meget; men Ahabs større, mørkere og dybere side er endnu ikke engang antydet. Det er dog nytteløst at gøre dybsindigheder folkelige, og al sandhed er dybsindig. Langt nede, snoende sig ned fra selve hjertet af dette pigbesatte Hôtel de Cluny, hvor vi nu står — hvor storslået og vidunderligt det end er, så forlad det nu — tag vejen, I ædlere og sørgmodigere sjæle, til de enorme romerske haller i Thermes (de gamle bade nedenunder), hvor langt under menneskets fantastiske tårne på jordens overflade hans rod af storhed, hele hans frygtelige væsen sidder i skægget pomp: en oldtidsskikkelse begravet under oldtider og tronende på torsoer! Således håner de store guder den fangne konge med en brudt trone; således sidder han tålmodigt som en karyatide (en udhugget skikkelse, der tjener som søjle) og bærer på sin frosne pande tidsalderes opstablede arkitraver. Find vejen derned, I stoltere og sørgmodigere sjæle! Spørg den stolte, sørgmodige konge! En familielighed! Ja, han avlede jer, I unge landflygtige kongebørn; og kun fra jeres dystre far vil den gamle statshemmelighed komme.

Nu havde Ahab i sit hjerte en glimtvis fornemmelse af dette — nemlig: alle mine midler er sunde, mit motiv og mit mål er vanvid. Men uden magt til at slå det ihjel, ændre det eller undslippe det vidste han også, at han i lang tid havde bedraget menneskene med hensyn til det — og i nogle henseender stadig gjorde det. Men hans bedrag var kun underlagt hans bevidsthed, ikke hans overlagte vilje. Alligevel lykkedes det ham så godt, at da han endelig gik i land på sit elfenbensben, tænkte ingen nantucketer andet, end at han var naturligt sorgfuld, og det dybt, over den forfærdelige ulykke, der var overgået ham.

Beretningerne om hans uomtvistelige vanvid på havet blev ligeledes almindeligvis tilskrevet en beslægtet årsag. Og det gjorde alt det ekstra tungsind, som siden altid, lige til dagen da han sejlede med Pequod på den nuværende rejse, sad og rugede på hans pande. Og det er ikke så usandsynligt, at de beregnende folk på den kloge ø, langt fra at tvivle på hans egnethed til endnu en hvalfangerrejse på grund af så mørke symptomer, var tilbøjelige til at mene, at han netop derfor var så meget desto bedre egnet og skærpet til en jagt, der er så fuld af raseri og vildskab som den blodige hvaljagt. Gnavet indvendig og svedet udvendig af de ubevægelige, ubarmhjertige hugtænder fra en ulægelig idé — sådan en mand, hvis han kunne findes, ville se ud til at være den rette til at slynge sit jern og løfte sin lanse mod den mest skrækindjagende af alle bæster. Eller, hvis man af en eller anden grund anså ham for fysisk uegnet til det, ville sådan en mand se ud til at være ypperligt egnet til at opmuntre og hyle sine underordnede ind i angrebet. Men lad nu alt dette være, som det vil; så meget er sikkert: Med sit vanvittige, uformindskede raseris hemmelighed lukket inde i sig med slå og lås havde Ahab bevidst sejlet på den nuværende rejse med det ene, altopslugende mål at jage den Hvide Hval. Havde nogen af hans gamle bekendte i land bare halvt drømt om, hvad der lurede i ham dengang, hvor hurtigt ville deres forfærdede og retskafne sjæle så ikke have revet skibet væk fra sådan en djævelsk mand! De var ude efter indbringende togter, med fortjenesten talt op i dollars fra mønten. Han var ude efter en dristig, ubønhørlig og overnaturlig hævn.

Her var altså denne gråhårede, ugudelige gamle mand, som med forbandelser jagede en Jobs hval rundt om jorden, og endda i spidsen for et mandskab, der for størstedelen bestod af bastardrenegater og skibbrudne og kannibaler — et mandskab, som også var moralsk svækket af, at ren dyd og retsindighed uden hjælp var magtesløs hos Starbuck, af den usårlige lystighed hos Stubb, der skyldtes ligegyldighed og letsind, og af den gennemtrængende middelmådighed hos Flask. Et sådant mandskab, med sådanne officerer, så ud til at være særligt udvalgt og pakket af en eller anden helvedes skæbne for at hjælpe ham til hans monomane hævn. Hvordan det kunne være, at de svarede så rigeligt på den gamle mands raseri — ved hvilken ond magi deres sjæle var besatte, så hans had til tider næsten var deres, og den Hvide Hval lige så meget deres uudholdelige fjende som hans — hvordan alt dette kunne ske — hvad den Hvide Hval var for dem, eller hvordan han også for deres ubevidste forstand på en dunkel, uanet måde kunne have tedet sig som den glidende store dæmon i livets have — at forklare alt dette ville være at dykke dybere, end Ishmael kan. Minearbejderen under jorden, der arbejder i os alle — hvordan kan nogen sige, hvor hans skakt fører hen, ud fra den evigt skiftende, dæmpede lyd af hans hakke? Hvem mærker ikke den uimodståelige arm, der trækker? Hvilken jolle på slæb efter et linjeskib (et skib med fireoghalvfjerds kanoner) kan stå stille? For min egen del gav jeg mig hen til tidens og stedets tøjlesløshed. Men mens jeg stadig i en fart var på vej til at møde hvalen, kunne jeg ikke se andet i det bæst end det dødeligste onde.
